title: Cellular: low latency and no stalls on a mobile network
description:
## Goal
phonepad stays responsive when the phone is on a cellular network: low glass-to-glass latency, no stalls, graceful quality loss when bandwidth drops. Today flow control allows 4 unacknowledged units, so at 150 ms RTT the stream is capped near 4/0.15 ≈ 26 units/s, every unit is CQP 24 regardless of link capacity, an IDR is ~40 KB, and the transport is WebSocket over TCP through tailscale serve (head-of-line blocking under loss, possible DERP relay).

## Operator decision
2026-11-09, verbatim: "One thing to consider is we should optimize the rendering for the latency, because I think I will be on the cell phone network, so we need to make sure that we handle this case. So this is a to-do. This is not that has to be done immediately. This is something that you should plan for. Feel free to file the beads, and I think you can start delegating to subagents this task when you feel ready." Earlier the same day: "be bold and experiment", "we can just fork and fix things", "address all gaps and limitations, accept all", "no legacy code". Approves: new dependencies, domain type and wire protocol changes, pad.html changes, transport changes. Nothing else; children inherit this.

## Children
Instrument first (every other child measures against it), then flow control, adaptive quality, keyframe smoothing, latency hiding on the phone, transport and path spikes.

## Oracle
All children closed; on the latency harness at emulated 150 ms RTT / 5 Mbit/s: ≥ 50 units/s while the pointer moves and capture→ack p95 ≤ RTT + 80 ms; operator judges it usable from a phone on cellular (human judgement, Iouri, on his phone).

title: Latency harness: per-stage timing and a network emulator
description:
## What
A measurement harness for latency under network conditions, usable by every other child:
- Each access unit carries an id and its capture time; the page reports per unit when it was received, decoded and drawn (in its ack or a separate report); the server computes per stage: capture→send, send→ack (network + decode), and units/s, bytes/s, stalls (> 250 ms with no drawn frame).
- A network emulator in front of the test instance (127.0.0.1:8766): configurable one-way delay, jitter, bandwidth cap and packet loss (TCP-level emulation in userspace is acceptable; netem needs root, which we don't use).
- `cargo xtask latency <profile>` runs the test instance + emulator + pointer mover + fake clients (fakeh264-style, or headless Chromium running the real page) and prints p50/p95/max per stage. Profiles at least: lan (0 ms), wifi (10 ms, 50 Mbit/s), lte (60 ms ±20, 10 Mbit/s), bad-lte (150 ms ±50, 3 Mbit/s, 1% loss).
## Oracle
- Known-case check (cm-27o): with the emulator set to added RTT D ∈ {0, 100, 200} ms, measured send→ack p50 rises by D ± 15 ms; with a 2 Mbit/s cap, measured bytes/s ≤ 2.1 Mbit/s.
- The printed table for all four profiles is recorded in the bead as the baseline for the other children.

title: Flow control collapses on busy content: desync and keyframe loop
description:
## What
With busy content (1-4 KB deltas) the transport spike measured every transport collapsing to 10-26 units/s with 64-125 desyncs a minute at bad-lte (ADR 0007, busy row) — flow control (ADR 0005), not the transport. A desync costs a keyframe wait (>= 500 ms spacing) and a 40 KB keyframe, which refills the pipe and desyncs again. Find the loop and break it (e.g. drop to the latest delta instead of desyncing when only the queue is full, rate-adapt (r9c.3) before the pipe fills, pace keyframes to the delivery rate).
## Oracle
On the nested harness with busy content (the spike's 1-4 KB delta profile, or nested content at 60 Hz over a large area) at bad-lte: desyncs <= 5 per minute and units/s >= 80% of the lte figure, 60 s, 2 runs at load < 3; lan unchanged ±10%. Red today: 64-125 desyncs/min, 10-26 units/s.

title: Flow control sized to the link (RTT and delivery rate)
description:
## What
Flow control sized to the link instead of a fixed 4 units: the number of unacknowledged units/bytes a viewer may have adapts to the measured RTT and delivery rate (bandwidth-delay product), with a bound on queueing delay so latency doesn't build up. Keep the core invariants: a viewer never receives a delta without its reference; a stalled viewer never affects others; keyframe requests only when the viewer can take one. Lives in phonepad-core as a sum-type state machine with pure decide/evolve (cm-prk).
## Oracle
On the latency harness: lte profile ≥ 55 units/s and send→ack p95 ≤ RTT + 60 ms; bad-lte profile no stall > 500 ms in a 60 s run; lan profile unchanged from baseline (± 5%). Today (red): lte is capped near 4/RTT.

title: Adaptive quality: QP and rate follow delivered throughput
description:
## What
Adaptive quality: the encoder's per-unit quantizer (CQP allows per-frame QP) and, if needed, frame rate and output scale follow the delivered throughput, so the queue stays short on a slow link and quality returns when the link recovers. One encoder serves all viewers, so the policy must define what happens with viewers on different links (e.g. follow the slowest synced viewer, or per-viewer layers — choose and justify).
## Oracle
Harness with a 2 Mbit/s cap: send→ack p95 ≤ RTT + 100 ms and no stall > 500 ms; switch the cap to 20 Mbit/s mid-run: QP returns to its base within 5 s. Worst-frame PSNR at the base QP unchanged (h264-check). Today (red): at 2 Mbit/s the queue grows without bound or units are dropped en masse.

title: Keyframes without bursts on join and desync
description:
## What
Keyframes without bursts: a joining or desynced viewer today gets a ~40 KB IDR, which takes ~160 ms at 2 Mbit/s. Smooth this (e.g. periodic intra refresh / gradual decoder refresh instead of IDR on join, or a lower-QP IDR) while keeping "a viewer never receives a delta without its reference" true and verifiable.
## Oracle
Harness bad-lte: time from join to first drawn frame p95 ≤ 2×RTT + 150 ms; largest unit ≤ 3× median unit during steady state; h264-check still passes; WebCodecs on the phone (operator, Iouri) decodes it.

title: Latency hiding on the phone: predicted pointer and local pan
description:
## What
Latency hiding on the phone: pointer feedback must not wait for the network. The page moves the pointer ring immediately on touch (predicted from the moves it sent) and shifts the last drawn frame locally by the predicted pan, reconciling when the server's unit for that position arrives (units carry the cursor and region they were cropped at). Optionally the server sends a margin around the view so local pans reveal real pixels.
## Oracle
In the page (performance.now): touch→ring-redraw p95 ≤ 20 ms regardless of profile, measured on the harness with headless Chromium; on bad-lte the ring never jumps backwards more than 4 px at reconciliation; operator (Iouri) judges pointer feel on cellular acceptable.

comments.author: elendal
comments.text: Implemented on branch cell-5 (worktree scratchpad/wt-c5), 9 commits 72d9eb6..fca5122, not pushed/merged. Design: each move carries seq s (per connection, from 1); input thread records a phone's last written move inside a seqlock (marks::Marks, generation odd while writing); the sampler keeps a cursorpos reading only if the generation was even and unchanged across copy+query, so a position is credited with exactly the moves written before it (first version without the generation: 4/256 lan messages jumped back, 3 of them by one whole 6 px move double-counted). Pointer message 9 -> 29 bytes: x,y, phone's last applied seq, monitor x,y,w,h. Page (pointer.js, pure, node --test under new page-tests gate): prediction = heard position + uncredited moves, each clamped to the monitor; ring + pan redrawn on the next frame from the last decoded window (pad colour outside it). Oracle: cargo xtask latency touch (CDP Input.dispatchTouchEvent, mover off), tip run seconds=10: handler->redraw p95 lan 0.7 / wifi 0.5 / lte 0.6 / bad-lte 0.5 ms (<=20 PASS); largest backward jump at reconciliation lan 0.0 / wifi 0.0 / lte 0.0 / bad-lte 0.3 px; bad-lte 30 s: p95 0.6 ms, backward max 1.0 px over 676 messages (<=4 PASS). Event-timestamp->redraw p50 ~33 ms on every profile = headless Chromium input pipeline, profile-independent. Known cases: 30 ms busy paint -> redraw FAIL (p95 30.6); page forgetting in-flight moves -> lte jump FAIL (7.8 px). Open for operator: Hyprland libinput adaptive accel also accelerates the phonepad device (2px/16ms x0.9, 10px x1.1, 25px x2.0) so at speed the ring jumps FORWARD at reconciliation (max 45-62 px on bad-lte bursts); making the device flat + retuning page accel is a feel decision, not taken. Optional view margin not built. Feel on cellular: operator. Mutation: cargo-mutants on branch diff 173 mutants, 92 caught/42 missed/39 unviable before follow-up tests; after them touch.rs+cursor.rs 69 caught/12 missed (all CDP/hyprctl I/O shells); JS hand mutants 31/31 killed. ADR 0006.

title: Spike: transports better than WebSocket over TCP under loss
description:
## What
Spike, time box 1 day: transport alternatives to WebSocket-over-TCP through tailscale serve for cellular: WebTransport (HTTP/3, unreliable datagrams), WebRTC data channels or video track, a direct tailnet connection (not through `tailscale serve`) — what each costs in code, deps and the auth model (today: Tailscale-User-Login header from tailscale serve), and what it buys under loss.
## Oracle
A written comparison in this bead with measurements on the harness at bad-lte (1% loss): stall count and p95 send→draw for WebSocket vs the best alternative prototype; recommendation with the condition that would reverse it. The operator decides whether to adopt.

comments.author: elendal
comments.text:
Spike result (branch cell-6, 3 commits, not merged/pushed; full write-up docs/adr/0007-transport-spike.md, Status: Proposed). Bead stays open: the operator decides adoption.

Built: `cargo xtask transport` (crates/xtask/src/transport*). One process replays a synthetic unit stream (unit every 20 ms, deltas 200-600 B, 40 KB keyframes >= 500 ms apart) through phonepad-core's flow control to a Rust viewer that releases units in decode order, acks them, and pings every 20 ms. Arms: ws-proxy (WebSocket through the harness's TCP emulator), wt-relay (WebTransport via wtransport 0.7.2/quinn: one uni stream per unit, acks and pings on their own streams, 1200-byte QUIC payloads, Cubic or BBR, through a new userspace UDP emulator), ws-direct/wt-direct (kernel netem in `unshare -rn`, same knobs: real Linux TCP and real quinn against the same real loss). Rust client, not the page: the page's software decoder would hide the transport. Headless Chromium 155 smoke (`serve-wt`): connected with serverCertificateHashes to wtransport's self-signed ECDSA P-256 14-day cert and acked 477 units in order. Pixel 7a: not tried.

UDP emulator known case (`transport calibrate`): PASS +100.1 / +200.1 ms added RTT (+-5); 1.14% of 20000 datagrams lost at 1% set (3 sigma 0.21%); 2.000 Mbit/s through a 2 Mbit/s cap with overflows; 150+-50 ms RTTs within [100,205]. Planted mutants turn it red (half delay: +50/+100; no loss: 0.000%). netem cross-check: 0.86% loss, RTT p50 181 vs relay 169. ws-proxy reproduces ADR 0005 bad-lte acking viewer (longest gap 348-357 vs 344-375, send->ack p95 456-470 vs 439-449).

bad-lte (150+-50 ms, 3 Mbit/s, 1%), 60 s, loadavg < 3 at each start, 2 rounds:
| arm | stalls >250/>500 | longest gap | send->draw p95 | ping RTT p95 | units/s |
| ws-proxy (modelled 300 ms stall) | 43/0, 43/0 | 357, 348 | 323, 324 | 456, 456 | 50.1 |
| wt-relay Cubic | 6/0, 5/0 | 319, 303 | 199, 217 | 336, 321 | 50.0 |
| wt-relay BBR | 1/0, 1/0 | 342, 256 | 172, 177 | 302, 314 | 50.0 |
| ws-direct netem (Linux TCP) | 3/0, 1/0 | 337, 251 | 248, 242 | 374, 367 | 50.0 |
| wt-direct netem Cubic | 11/1, 10/0 | 505, 302 | 230, 230 | 346, 346 | 50.0 |
| wt-direct netem BBR | 0/0, 0/0 | 246, 229 | 212, 135 | 337, 321 | 50.0 |
Busy content (deltas 1-4 KB, 1 round): every arm collapses to 10-26 units/s with 64-125 desyncs a minute (WS 20-22, WT BBR 20-26, WT Cubic 10-12). That is flow control, not transport.

Reading: the harness's TCP model overstates WebSocket stalls (43/min vs 1-3/min for real Linux TCP under the same real loss). The best alternative (WebTransport + BBR) beats real TCP by 1-3 stalls/min -> 0 and 30-110 ms send->draw p95; with quinn's default Cubic it is worse than TCP.

Costs: tailscale serve is TCP only (--https/--http/--tcp/--tls-terminated-tcp), so phonepad would bind UDP on its tailnet IP and authenticate itself: LocalAPI whois on the peer ip:port (refuse tagged nodes) or a short-lived token minted by the header-authenticated page (keeps today's trusted boundary). Certs: tailscale cert renewed by phonepad, or 14-day self-signed + serverCertificateHashes delivered by the page. DERP is TCP, so no gain there; a WebSocket fallback stays. ~300-500 server + ~100 page lines; 105 new lockfile entries (quinn, rustls, ring...); quinn BBR is marked experimental. Datagrams and WebRTC not prototyped (reference chain makes unreliable delivery cost keyframes; WebRTC video track leaves WebCodecs; WebRTC's auth would ride the existing WS as signaling).

Recommendation: do not adopt now. First fix the harness's TCP loss model (or run it under netem) and the busy-content flow-control collapse.
Reversal condition: the real downlink TCP sender is tailscaled's userspace netstack, not Linux. If it recovers like the model (> ~10 stalls >250 ms/min at 1% loss, measured from the phone on a direct cellular path or with netem under a tailscale serve path on a test node), or r9c.7 finds a direct cellular path with loss well above 1%, WebTransport + BBR wins and the costs are worth paying.

comments.text: Addendum: known case for the netem TCP arm. 15 s ws-direct under netem: qdisc sent 4994 packets, dropped 49 (0.98%); /proc/net/snmp OutSegs 5031, RetransSegs 35, so Linux TCP met netem one segment per packet and the 1-3 stalls/min figure is per-segment 1% loss. netem's ordering with rate+jitter not verified.

title: Spike: phone-to-desktop path on cellular (direct vs DERP)
description:
## What
Spike, time box 2 hours: the real path from the phone on cellular to the desktop. Is it direct or through a DERP relay (`tailscale status` shows "relay"), what RTT and bandwidth does it give (`tailscale ping`, iperf over the tailnet), and what makes it direct (UDP port mapping, router config, peer relay through a tagged node that already connects directly).
## Oracle
Measured RTT and throughput from the phone on cellular to the desktop recorded here, with path type; the harness profiles (child 1) adjusted to match; if relayed, a concrete step to get a direct path and its measured effect. Needs the operator's phone on cellular (Iouri runs the phone side).

title: One encode per content change: distinct changes/s reach 60
description:
## What
Each change inside the encoded window is encoded twice: both ext-image-copy-capture sessions report it and their frames carry different timestamps (ADR 0004, open question). On the nested harness at 125 Hz content, main sends ~56 units/s but only ~35-41 distinct content changes/s reach the viewer. An uncommitted experiment with one capture session removed the duplicates and reached 58.5 changes/s in one run (50.6 in another). Make every content change cost one encode and raise distinct changes/s, without giving up the frame rate the two sessions bought (one frame in flight per session in Hyprland).
## Oracle
`cargo xtask latency nested calibrate` passes its 125 Hz clause (changes/s = 60 ± 10%) in 2 of 2 runs started at load < 3, and the 20 Hz clause shows units/s = changes/s (± 5%, no duplicates). Red today: main gives 34.8 and 35.7 changes/s at 125 Hz and 39.7 units/s for 19.9 changes/s at 20 Hz.

comments.author: elendal
comments.text:
Branch cell-8 (worktree scratchpad/wt-c8) on main 9b37443, not merged, not closed. Commits: 5311d57 slot tests move to plan/tests/slots.rs (pure move); 0249454 capture: one frame waits for a commit (code, tests, README, ADR 0004 section 'One frame waits for a commit').

Diagnosis (trace of main, nested 125 Hz): both sessions' frames were requested within 15 us and copied in the same output commit (presentation_time 0.1-0.2 ms apart = Hyprland's steadyNow per copy), ready 12-15 ms later, then both reissued: ~35 commits/s captured, each encoded twice. Move: Slot = Requested | Copying{stamp} | Held | Free; to_issue returns at most one (slot, session) and none while a slot is Requested, so the next frame is requested at the previous one's presentation_time and waits for the next commit while the other session still copies. Rejected: stamp dedup (no commit identity; stamps differ per frame), damage dedup (stock = full damage), one session (58.5/50.6, r9c.2), three sessions (50.4 in one run).

A/B nested calibrate / nested hz=125 viewer lte, alternating, load<3 at start (1.4-3.0 start, 1.4-3.8 end), changes/s (units/s):

Oracle: 20 Hz clause MET (units = changes in every run). 125 Hz clause NOT MET 2/2: bimodal 59 vs 52, 3 of 8 A/B runs pass. Cause measured: trace shows the next request pending within 0.1 ms of the previous presentation_time yet copied 33 ms later in ~10% of intervals; a probe logging the content client's frame callbacks matched 545/551 copies to a nested render within 2 ms and vice versa, i.e. every render was captured and the rate is the nested compositor's render rate (that run 36.7/s while being stopped). One probe run, partial; needs a repeat on an invisible (headless) nested compositor.

title: Harness: calibrate the TCP loss model to real TCP
description:
## What
The transport spike (r9c.6, ADR 0007) found the latency harness's TCP loss model (userspace proxy: a lost segment arrives max(200 ms, 2xRTT) later and everything behind it waits) produces ~43 stalls > 250 ms a minute at bad-lte, while real Linux TCP under kernel netem with the same 1% per-segment loss shows 1-3. Every cellular decision is measured against this model, so it overstates TCP's cost. Replace it with a model calibrated to real TCP (e.g. run the harness's link under netem in an unprivileged user+net namespace, as the spike's ws-direct arm did), keeping the existing profiles and known cases.
## Oracle
`cargo xtask latency calibrate` still passes; a new known case at bad-lte (1% loss) shows stalls > 250 ms per minute within 2x of the netem ws-direct arm in ADR 0007 (1-3/min) for the same synthetic stream, 2 runs at load < 3. Red today: 43/min.
